output.title: Measure list hygiene before you automate it
output.body:
If you want to measure list hygiene, make it a bounded workflow decision, not a vague “clean up the list” project. Pick one visible problem first: bounce rate, unsubscribe trend, complaint rate, or a drop in engagement. Then decide what action that metric would trigger. If the answer is “not much,” you are probably measuring for comfort, not control.

In most small businesses, the first pass does not need AI. List-quality signals are usually rule-based: bounces, unsubscribes, and complaint feedback already live in the reporting your email tool provides. A simple pivot table can be enough to see whether the list is drifting. AI only becomes relevant if you want help classifying complaint reasons, spotting patterns in older feedback, or grouping contacts by engagement. That is a separate task from measuring list hygiene itself.

A useful diagnostic question is: “What would I do differently if I knew this list was getting worse?” If the answer is concrete — remove bounces, pause a re-engagement send, suppress a segment — then the metric has a job. If the answer is vague, the metric is just a dashboard ornament. Nice to look at, not very helpful.

For a practical next step, export the current list report and write down one threshold you would actually act on. Keep the threshold simple, note the action beside it, and check whether the data reaches the decision before you think about automation. Measurement without a decision is just tidying the spreadsheet. Test the threshold first; automate later, if it still earns its place.
